screens.title: Application Security Testing
screens.narratorSegment: Application security testing is the feedback loop that turns secure design into secure reality. In this lesson you will learn the main testing methodologies — static, dynamic, interactive, runtime protection, fuzzing, and manual penetration testing — and why each one matters at different stages of the software development lifecycle. We will show practical ways to choose tools, interpret test results, and automate testing in CI/CD so security becomes routine instead of a last-minute gate. For example, running a static analysis on every commit finds coding patterns that indicate buffer overflows, while a dynamic scan against a running staging server reveals runtime misconfigurations and exploitable endpoints. You will see how interactive testing blends both views and how runtime self-protection can stop an attack in production. By the end, you’ll know which test to run when, how to prioritize findings based on exploitability and impact, and how to avoid common mistakes like over-relying on a single tool or failing to retest after fixes. Consider which part of your pipeline would benefit most from automated tests today.

screens.title: Static Application Security Testing (SAST)
screens.narratorSegment: Static Application Security Testing, or SAST, inspects code artifacts without running them. It looks for known vulnerable patterns in source code, bytecode or compiled binaries and highlights exact locations so developers can remediate early. A practical example is scanning a C++ module to flag possible buffer overflows or unvalidated input patterns before the code ships. The major advantage is early detection: run SAST during development or in commit hooks and you often fix issues when the code context is fresh. Be mindful of two common misconceptions: first, SAST is not a proof of exploitability — it reports patterns that may or may not be reachable at runtime. Second, SAST can produce false positives; you should tune rules and triage findings with developer context. In practice, integrate SAST into IDE plugins and CI jobs, configure rule sets for your language and frameworks, and combine SAST results with unit test coverage so you focus on true positives. Key takeaway: SAST is a precise, early detector of code-level weaknesses but must be paired with runtime tests to confirm exploitability. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) means analyze code artifacts before execution to find code-level flaws and give line-of-code remediation guidance.. In practical terms, white-box analysis of source, bytecode or binaries before execution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept Static Application Security Testing
SAST — Static Analysis
Inspect source, bytecode, or binaries to find patterns that indicate vulnerabilities.
How it works
  • Parse source or bytecode and scan for vulnerable patterns and insecure APIs.
  • Provide exact file and line references to guide developer fixes.
  • Run in IDE, pre-commit hooks, or CI to 'shift left'.
Common advantages
Early detection, precise remediation hints, works without a running environment.
Common pitfalls
  • False positives require triage.
  • May miss runtime-only issues and configuration faults.
Key Takeaway

SAST finds code-level issues early and gives precise lines to fix, but it should be paired with runtime tests to confirm exploitability.

Concrete example
A SAST tool scans a C++ codebase and flags a function using unsafe string copy without bounds checks. The tool points to the source line and suggests using a safer API or adding explicit length checks. The team fixes the code, runs unit tests, and the SAST rule passes on the next commit.
Misconception check
SAST reports do not guarantee exploitability. Treat them as precise hints to inspect execution context or add tests that exercise that code path.
Tool examples (from chapter)
SonarQube, Checkmarx, Fortify, Snyk for dependencies.

screens.title: SAST vs DAST vs IAST — Choosing the right view
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between SAST, DAST and IAST requires understanding what each method sees and when that visibility is most valuable. SAST reads code artifacts and catches coding patterns early; DAST interacts with a running application and reveals what an attacker can reach; IAST instruments the application at runtime and combines code-level insight with real execution context. A concrete example: SAST may flag an S Q L concatenation pattern, DAST can verify whether an exposed endpoint accepts exploit strings, and IAST can point to the exact function and input flow that allowed the injection. Common pitfalls include over-relying on a single method — SAST alone may miss runtime misconfigurations, DAST alone may not reach unexercised code paths, and IAST requires instrumentation and suitable test coverage to be effective. Use this contrast to build complementary layers: SAST on commit, DAST in staging and production testing, and IAST during functional testing to reduce false positives and speed remediation. End with this question: where in your pipeline are you missing one of these views? SAST vs DAST vs IAST — Choosing the right view means sast finds code issues early, dast validates exploitability at runtime, and iast connects code to execution for accurate guidance.. In practical terms, contrast capabilities, timing, and common blind spots. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: SAST finds code issues early, DAST validates exploitability at runtime, and IAST connects code to execution for accurate guidance.

content.html:
Comparison SAST · DAST · IAST
Choosing the right view
Understand how timing and visibility affect what you can detect and fix.
SAST
White-box; static code analysis; early in SSDLC.
  • Finds code patterns and insecure APIs.
  • Precise line-of-code remediation guidance.
  • False positives require triage.
DAST
Black-box; tests the running app via interfaces; useful in staging or production testing.
  • Validates exploitability of endpoints.
  • Lower false positives for reachable issues.
  • Cannot see unexercised or internal-only code paths.
IAST
Instrumented runtime that correlates code paths with live traffic.
  • High accuracy with low false positives.
  • Requires agents and good functional testing coverage.
  • Bridges SAST precision and DAST context.
Example scenario
SAST flags unsafe query construction, DAST verifies the endpoint accepts malicious input, IAST shows the exact parameter flow responsible.
Misconception
A single tool will not provide full coverage. Use layered testing to reduce blind spots.
Tip
Run IAST during automated functional tests to maximize its effectiveness and reduce noise.

screens.title: Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST)
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic Application Security Testing analyzes the application while it is running. DAST tools send requests and observe how the app responds to detect issues such as cross-site scripting, S Q L injection, authentication bypasses and insecure headers. A concrete scenario: run a DAST scan against a staging server and the tool interacts with web forms and endpoints to see if unescaped output appears in responses. One key advantage is practical exploitability—DAST targets what an attacker can reach, lowering some classes of false positives. Common misconceptions include thinking DAST can find every vulnerability; it can only exercise reachable paths and depends heavily on crawling and coverage. You must also be careful when running DAST in production because active scans can trigger side effects. In practice use DAST in staging or against isolated test instances, complement it with manual verification for complex logic, and review findings with evidence and request/response traces to prioritize remediation. This approach focuses you on what matters to real attackers. Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) means run dast against a live application to find vulnerabilities that manifest at runtime and demonstrate real exploitability.. In practical terms, black-box scanning of a running application to find exploitable behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DAST in practice
keyIdea.text: Run DAST against a live application to find vulnerabilities that manifest at runtime and demonstrate real exploitability.

content.html:
Definition Dynamic Application Security Testing
DAST — Runtime Scanning
Interact with an application to reveal vulnerabilities that require execution to appear.
Typical findings
  • Cross-site scripting visible in responses.
  • SQL injection visible via error messages or behavior.
  • Authentication or session management bypasses.
Lab-ready example
Use OWASP ZAP's Automated Scan against a local app and review the Sites tree and Alerts to see evidence and suggested fixes.
Caution

Active DAST can produce traffic with side effects. Prefer staging or isolated environments unless you understand the impact.

How to analyze results
Review alerts with request and response evidence, reproduce issues manually to validate exploitability, and prioritize fixes that have high impact and high confidence.
Tool examples
OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite, Acunetix as referenced in the chapter.
Key Takeaway

DAST confirms what an attacker can reach, but requires good crawling and test coverage to find all exposed paths.

screens.title: DAST Lab Walkthrough with OWASP ZAP
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough guides you through a basic DAST scan using OWASP ZAP against a local application. Start by ensuring your test app is running on the local port, for example on localhost:5000. Open ZAP and choose the Automated Scan option. Enter the target URL and start the attack. ZAP will populate a Sites tree as it crawls and then produce Alerts for potential issues. A concrete practice: after an automated scan, review an XSS alert and inspect the evidence—request parameters and the exact response fragment that contains unescaped input. If ZAP lists an alert with evidence, reproduce it manually in a browser or via a simple HTTP request to confirm exploitability. In some cases, spidering or AJAX spidering will discover additional endpoints; run spidering and then an Active Scan on newly discovered paths. Remember that automated scans are a starting point: they produce evidence, not final verdicts. Prioritize alerts by severity and confidence, and retest after fixes. This flow converts a raw scan into actionable remediation steps you can apply in a pipeline or as part of release checks. DAST Lab Walkthrough with OWASP ZAP means run automated scan, inspect sites and alerts, reproduce evidence, spider for more paths, and retest after remediation.. In practical terms, a practical checklist to perform an automated scan and interpret alerts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DAST checklist
keyIdea.text: Run automated scan, inspect Sites and Alerts, reproduce evidence, spider for more paths, and retest after remediation.

content.html:
Process FlowDAST Lab
DAST Walkthrough — OWASP ZAP
Step-by-step checklist to run an automated scan and interpret results.
Steps
  1. Start the target web application locally and note its URL, for example http://localhost:5000.
  2. Open OWASP ZAP and choose Automated Scan, enter the target URL and click Attack.
  3. Watch the Sites tree populate as ZAP crawls; allow spidering to discover additional paths.
  4. Open the Alerts tab and inspect each alert's evidence: sample request and response data.
  5. Reproduce high-confidence issues manually to validate exploitability, then record reproduction steps for the developer.
  6. After fixes, rerun the scan and verify that alerts no longer appear or that evidence is removed.
Quick verification example (HTTP)
curl -i -X GET "http://localhost:5000/search?q=<script>alert(1)</script>"
Inspect the response for unescaped input as supporting evidence for XSS findings.
Interpretation tips
  • Prioritize alerts with high severity and high confidence first.
  • Use request/response evidence to create a minimal repro for developers.
  • Note side effects; if an alert modifies data, run scans in isolated test environments.
Check your understanding
After an automated scan you find an alert for information disclosure with low confidence. What would you do first? Reproduce the issue manually to confirm before flagging it as a blocker.
Key Takeaway

Automated DAST gives evidence; verification and reproduction are required to make findings actionable.

screens.title: Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST)
screens.narratorSegment: Interactive Application Security Testing operates inside the application during execution by instrumenting code or using agents. IAST watches data flow, stack traces and runtime context to detect vulnerabilities with accuracy and low false positives. For example, when functional tests exercise a login flow, an IAST agent can show that a particular method failed to validate input coming from a parameter, and it can point to the exact file and line involved. That combination of code-level detail and runtime visibility reduces wasted developer time spent chasing false positives. However, IAST requires deployment of agents and relies on test coverage: if a function is never exercised, IAST cannot inspect it. Use IAST in QA or test environments where functional tests run frequently, and correlate IAST findings with SAST and DAST outputs to build confidence. One misconception is to treat IAST as a replacement for SAST or DAST — instead, treat it as a high-precision bridge that helps pinpoint remediations in complex applications. Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST) means iast combines runtime context with code visibility to produce accurate findings and direct remediation guidance.. In practical terms, instrumented runtime analysis that links code paths to live requests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: IAST advantage
keyIdea.text: IAST combines runtime context with code visibility to produce accurate findings and direct remediation guidance.

content.html:
Core ConceptInteractive Application Security Testing
IAST — Instrumented Runtime
Monitor execution and link findings to code with high precision.
How IAST operates
  • Deploy an agent or instrument the application runtime.
  • Monitor data flow, method calls and HTTP traffic during tests.
  • Correlate runtime evidence with specific code locations.
When to use
Run in QA during automated functional tests to reduce false positives and get exact remediation pointers.
Benefits and limits
  • High accuracy and actionable remediation guidance.
  • Requires instrumentation and sufficient test coverage.
  • Not a full replacement for SAST or DAST.
Example tool references
Contrast Security and HCL AppScan are examples discussed in the chapter.
Key Takeaway

IAST gives the best of both worlds for tested code paths: actionable findings with low false positives, when test coverage exists.

screens.title: Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP)
screens.narratorSegment: Runtime Application Self-Protection is a defensive technology that runs inside the application and monitors behavior to detect and block attacks in real time. RASP acts like an immune system for the application: when it detects anomalies such as unexpected input patterns or sequences that match attack signatures, it can block requests, log evidence, and trigger alerts. A practical example is a RASP agent dropping a suspicious request that attempts a S Q L injection pattern and returning an error without exposing sensitive details. RASP is valuable in production because it provides immediate protection, including against zero-day techniques that reach the application. However, RASP can cause false positives if rules are too strict and may require tuning. It is not a substitute for fixing the underlying vulnerability; instead, treat RASP as mitigation and rapid response that reduces exposure while developers remediate the root cause. Consider RASP as a last-mile defense enabling safer production operations when combined with layered testing upstream. Runtime Application Self-Protection (RASP) means rasp blocks and alerts on suspected attacks at runtime but should complement, not replace, remediation and upstream testing.. In practical terms, in-process defense that detects and blocks attacks as they happen. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
DefinitionRuntime Application Self-Protection
RASP — Runtime Defense
Integrate protection into the application to detect and stop attacks in real time.
What RASP does
  • Monitor runtime behavior and data flow for attack patterns.
  • Block suspicious requests and alert security teams immediately.
  • Act as a mitigation while developers patch the root cause.
Production use
RASP is useful in production to reduce exposure, but it requires careful tuning to avoid disrupting legitimate traffic.
Benefits and trade-offs
  • Immediate protection against detected attacks.
  • May create false positives that require tuning.
  • Should not replace fixing vulnerabilities at the code level.
Analogy
Think of RASP as an on-site security guard who stops suspicious activity while the building owner repairs the broken lock.
Key Takeaway

RASP supplies real-time protection in production, reducing exposure but not replacing remediation upstream.

screens.title: Penetration Testing
screens.narratorSegment: Penetration testing is a manual, goal-focused exercise performed by skilled security professionals to simulate real-world attacks. The objective is to find complex vulnerabilities, logical flaws, and chained exploit scenarios that automated tools often miss. For instance, testers may combine an authentication bypass, a misconfigured A P I and an exposed admin endpoint to demonstrate a full attack chain that has business impact. Penetration testing typically occurs later in the SDLC—before release or after major changes—to give a realistic assessment of the application's security posture. Key characteristics include manual creativity, targeted reconnaissance, and demonstrating exploitability and business impact. A common misconception is that automated scanners replace penetration testing; they do not. Automated tools surface many issues, but a human tester examines logic, workflows and context that tools cannot reason about. Use penetration tests to validate that automated controls work, to test business logic, and to provide prioritized findings with exploit scenarios. Finish with a reflective question: what complex, business-impacting scenario could automation miss in your application? Penetration Testing means human testers find logic flaws and chained exploits, producing realistic risk assessments and remediation priorities.. In practical terms, manual, goal-oriented assessments to uncover complex, chained issues. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Core ConceptPenetration Testing
Penetration Testing — Manual Assessment
Simulate real attacks to find complex, chained vulnerabilities and demonstrate business impact.
Characteristics
  • Manual and creative testing by experienced analysts.
  • Focus on business logic, authentication, and chained exploits.
  • Deliverable: actionable report demonstrating exploitability and impact.
When to run
Before major releases or after significant architectural changes, and to validate automated testing results.
Common misconceptions
Pen tests do not replace automated scanning; they are complementary and provide realistic exploit demonstrations.
Key Takeaway

Penetration testing supplies human creativity to reveal vulnerabilities and attack chains that automated tools miss, and it helps quantify business risk.

screens.title: Fuzzing
screens.narratorSegment: Fuzzing is a testing technique that bombards an application with malformed, unexpected or random inputs to reveal crashes, memory corruption, or other input-handling faults. It is particularly effective against parsers, protocol handlers, and file-processing code. A concrete example is feeding malformed files into a document parser to trigger a buffer overflow that an ordinary functional test would not reach. Fuzzing can be automated at scale and sometimes uncovers obscure vulnerabilities that remain hidden for years. One important point is that fuzzing often finds a symptom — a crash or exception — but not the root cause; developers must analyze the crash to fix the underlying bug. Also, fuzzing may produce many non-security-related crashes, so triage and reproducibility are critical. Use fuzzing in components that process untrusted input and combine it with sanitizers and memory analysis tools to get precise diagnostics. In short, fuzzing surfaces low-level failures that traditional AST techniques may miss. Fuzzing means automate malformed inputs to find crashes and memory issues in parsers and input handlers; triage and analyze crashes to fix root causes.. In practical terms, stress inputs to discover crashes, buffer overflows, and parser faults. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

DefinitionFuzzing
Fuzzing — Input Stress Testing
Provide malformed inputs at scale to find crashes and memory corruption in code that handles untrusted data.
Targets
  • Parsers for file formats and protocols.
  • Network input handlers and protocol stacks.
  • Any code that ingests untrusted data.
Workflow
Run fuzzers with instrumentation, capture crashes, and analyze with debuggers or sanitizers to identify root causes.
Benefits and cautions
  • Finds obscure, often high-impact memory issues.
  • Produces many crashes that require triage and debugging.
  • Works best with good instrumentation and reproduction strategies.
Key Takeaway

Fuzzing reveals low-level input handling bugs and is essential for components that process untrusted data, but it requires careful triage and debugging to resolve findings.

screens.title: Integrating AST into CI/CD
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating application security testing into CI/CD automates the tests developers need and transforms security from a bottleneck into a continuous assurance practice. A practical pipeline looks like this: run SAST on every commit or pull request to catch code-level issues early; after successful builds deploy to a staging environment and trigger a DAST scan to validate runtime behavior; during QA run IAST agents alongside functional tests to get high-precision findings; finally, schedule periodic penetration testing and fuzzing for deep, manual and low-level coverage. When interpreting results in an automated pipeline, prioritize failures that block builds differently from informational alerts: severe, exploitable issues may require blocking deployments, while low-confidence findings can be ticketed for scheduled fixes. Common mistakes include running heavy scans in developer machines, failing to retest after fixes, or ignoring the need to tune rules and signatures. The goal is to provide timely, actionable feedback to developers and security teams so remediation is fast and releases remain secure. Integrating AST into CI/CD means run sast on commit, dast in staging, iast during functional tests, and schedule manual tests for deep coverage.. In practical terms, automate sast, dast and iast to create continuous security feedback. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. keyIdea.text: Run SAST on commit, DAST in staging, IAST during functional tests, and schedule manual tests for deep coverage.

content.html:
Process FlowCI/CD Integration
Integrate AST into CI/CD
Automate tests to shift security left and create continuous feedback for developers.
Pipeline pattern
  1. SAST on commit or pull request for immediate developer feedback.
  2. Build and deploy to staging when SAST passes.
  3. Run DAST against staging to validate runtime behavior and endpoints.
  4. Run IAST during integration/functional tests to capture code-level runtime issues.
  5. Schedule periodic fuzzing and penetration tests for deep logic and memory testing.
Best practices
  • Triage and categorize findings to prevent alert fatigue.
  • Retest after remediation to close the loop.
  • Tune rules and scan configurations to reduce false positives.
Example automation trigger
Configure CI to run SAST as a pre-merge gate, and to run DAST as a post-deploy job against an isolated staging environment.
Key Takeaway

Automating AST in CI/CD ensures security feedback is timely, consistent, and part of developers' normal workflow rather than an afterthought.

screens.title: Interpreting and Prioritizing Findings
screens.narratorSegment: Interpreting security test output is as critical as running the tests. A raw report can contain a mix of false positives, informational notes and high-confidence exploitable issues. Start triage by assessing three elements for each finding: severity, exploitability and business impact. Severity describes the technical consequence; exploitability answers whether an attacker can reach the vulnerability; business impact quantifies data loss, downtime or regulatory exposure. A concrete example is an exposed debug endpoint: it may have medium severity but high exploitability in production and a high business impact if it leaks credentials. Use those dimensions to decide if a finding should block a release, be scheduled for a patch, or accepted with compensating controls like RASP. Common mistakes include failing to retest after remediation or relying solely on a single tool's confidence score. Always attach reproduction steps and evidence to tickets so developers can reproduce and verify fixes. End by asking: which three findings would you fix first and why? Interpreting and Prioritizing Findings means prioritize by severity, exploitability, and business impact; require reproduction evidence and retest after fixes.. In practical terms, turn scan output into actionable remediation with impact-aware triage. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Prioritize by severity, exploitability, and business impact; require reproduction evidence and retest after fixes.

content.html:
Process FlowTriage & Prioritization
Interpreting and Prioritizing Findings
A practical rubric to turn alerts into prioritized work items.
Triage dimensions
  • Severity — technical impact of the flaw.
  • Exploitability — how easily an attacker can reach it.
  • Business impact — data exposure, downtime or reputation risk.
Example prioritization
A critical SQL injection in a public API with proof-of-concept exploit is high priority. A low-confidence information leak on an internal endpoint may be scheduled for later triage.
Practical steps
  1. Reproduce the finding and record request/response evidence.
  2. Score severity, exploitability and business impact to prioritize.
  3. Create a ticket with reproducer and expected fix; retest after remediation.
Common mistakes
Ignoring retests, relying only on a tool's confidence score, or treating every alert as equally urgent.
Key Takeaway

Prioritization reduces noise and focuses fixes on the most exploitable, high-impact vulnerabilities; always require evidence and retesting.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: These core concepts will help you architect practical security testing. First, Application Security Testing is an umbrella term for complementary methods that together provide coverage across code, runtime and production. Second, SAST analyzes code artifacts early to give precise remediation guidance, while DAST validates what attackers can reach at runtime; use them together rather than in isolation. Third, IAST and RASP add runtime context: IAST links execution to code for accurate findings during testing, and RASP provides active defense in production. Keep these three concepts in mind as you design pipelines and choose tools: layering methods reduces blind spots, automation makes testing scalable, and human-led tests provide depth where automation cannot reach. Ask yourself which gaps remain in your current process and which combination of methods will close them most effectively.

fullNarratorScript:
Application security testing is the feedback loop that turns secure design into secure reality. In this lesson you will learn the main testing methodologies — static, dynamic, interactive, runtime protection, fuzzing, and manual penetration testing — and why each one matters at different stages of the software development lifecycle. We will show practical ways to choose tools, interpret test results, and automate testing in CI/CD so security becomes routine instead of a last-minute gate. For example, running a static analysis on every commit finds coding patterns that indicate buffer overflows, while a dynamic scan against a running staging server reveals runtime misconfigurations and exploitable endpoints. You will see how interactive testing blends both views and how runtime self-protection can stop an attack in production. By the end, you’ll know which test to run when, how to prioritize findings based on exploitability and impact, and how to avoid common mistakes like over-relying on a single tool or failing to retest after fixes. Consider which part of your pipeline would benefit most from automated tests today.

By the end of these first objective cards you will be able to identify and select the right testing approaches for different stages of development. First, you will differentiate SAST, DAST, IAST and RASP by what they inspect and when they run, so you can choose a tool that fits your development cadence. Second, you will select appropriate tools and techniques for the SSDLC: run SAST within the IDE or on commit, run DAST in staging or QA, and deploy IAST agents during functional testing. Third, you will learn to interpret test findings by assessing severity, exploitability, and business impact so remediation is prioritized correctly. Fourth, you will explain when manual penetration testing and fuzzing are necessary to find chained logic errors or obscure memory issues that automated tools miss. Each objective links a practical action to why it matters in reducing risk across the release pipeline. As you review these objectives, think which is most urgent in your current project and why.

This second objectives slide focuses on actionable skills you will practice. First, you will run a basic dynamic scan using OWASP ZAP against a local test application and learn how to read the Sites tree and Alerts to triage issues. Second, you will configure SAST to run on commit so developers receive immediate feedback inside their IDE or CI jobs. Third, you will integrate DAST steps into a staging pipeline to catch runtime issues before production. Fourth, you will apply prioritization heuristics: align severity, exploitability and business impact when deciding whether to block a release or schedule a patch. Each objective links a task to a concrete outcome: being able to run a scan, configure automation, interpret findings and set remediation priorities. These practical objectives map directly to the lab walkthrough and to production practices you can implement after completing this chapter.

Static Application Security Testing, or SAST, inspects code artifacts without running them. It looks for known vulnerable patterns in source code, bytecode or compiled binaries and highlights exact locations so developers can remediate early. A practical example is scanning a C++ module to flag possible buffer overflows or unvalidated input patterns before the code ships. The major advantage is early detection: run SAST during development or in commit hooks and you often fix issues when the code context is fresh. Be mindful of two common misconceptions: first, SAST is not a proof of exploitability — it reports patterns that may or may not be reachable at runtime. Second, SAST can produce false positives; you should tune rules and triage findings with developer context. In practice, integrate SAST into IDE plugins and CI jobs, configure rule sets for your language and frameworks, and combine SAST results with unit test coverage so you focus on true positives. Key takeaway: SAST is a precise, early detector of code-level weaknesses but must be paired with runtime tests to confirm exploitability. Static Application Security Testing (SAST) means analyze code artifacts before execution to find code-level flaws and give line-of-code remediation guidance.. In practical terms, white-box analysis of source, bytecode or binaries before execution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing between SAST, DAST and IAST requires understanding what each method sees and when that visibility is most valuable. SAST reads code artifacts and catches coding patterns early; DAST interacts with a running application and reveals what an attacker can reach; IAST instruments the application at runtime and combines code-level insight with real execution context. A concrete example: SAST may flag an S Q L concatenation pattern, DAST can verify whether an exposed endpoint accepts exploit strings, and IAST can point to the exact function and input flow that allowed the injection. Common pitfalls include over-relying on a single method — SAST alone may miss runtime misconfigurations, DAST alone may not reach unexercised code paths, and IAST requires instrumentation and suitable test coverage to be effective. Use this contrast to build complementary layers: SAST on commit, DAST in staging and production testing, and IAST during functional testing to reduce false positives and speed remediation. End with this question: where in your pipeline are you missing one of these views? SAST vs DAST vs IAST — Choosing the right view means sast finds code issues early, dast validates exploitability at runtime, and iast connects code to execution for accurate guidance.. In practical terms, contrast capabilities, timing, and common blind spots. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Dynamic Application Security Testing analyzes the application while it is running. DAST tools send requests and observe how the app responds to detect issues such as cross-site scripting, S Q L injection, authentication bypasses and insecure headers. A concrete scenario: run a DAST scan against a staging server and the tool interacts with web forms and endpoints to see if unescaped output appears in responses. One key advantage is practical exploitability—DAST targets what an attacker can reach, lowering some classes of false positives. Common misconceptions include thinking DAST can find every vulnerability; it can only exercise reachable paths and depends heavily on crawling and coverage. You must also be careful when running DAST in production because active scans can trigger side effects. In practice use DAST in staging or against isolated test instances, complement it with manual verification for complex logic, and review findings with evidence and request/response traces to prioritize remediation. This approach focuses you on what matters to real attackers. Dynamic Application Security Testing (DAST) means run dast against a live application to find vulnerabilities that manifest at runtime and demonstrate real exploitability.. In practical terms, black-box scanning of a running application to find exploitable behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This walkthrough guides you through a basic DAST scan using OWASP ZAP against a local application. Start by ensuring your test app is running on the local port, for example on localhost:5000. Open ZAP and choose the Automated Scan option. Enter the target URL and start the attack. ZAP will populate a Sites tree as it crawls and then produce Alerts for potential issues. A concrete practice: after an automated scan, review an XSS alert and inspect the evidence—request parameters and the exact response fragment that contains unescaped input. If ZAP lists an alert with evidence, reproduce it manually in a browser or via a simple HTTP request to confirm exploitability. In some cases, spidering or AJAX spidering will discover additional endpoints; run spidering and then an Active Scan on newly discovered paths. Remember that automated scans are a starting point: they produce evidence, not final verdicts. Prioritize alerts by severity and confidence, and retest after fixes. This flow converts a raw scan into actionable remediation steps you can apply in a pipeline or as part of release checks. DAST Lab Walkthrough with OWASP ZAP means run automated scan, inspect sites and alerts, reproduce evidence, spider for more paths, and retest after remediation.. In practical terms, a practical checklist to perform an automated scan and interpret alerts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Interactive Application Security Testing operates inside the application during execution by instrumenting code or using agents. IAST watches data flow, stack traces and runtime context to detect vulnerabilities with accuracy and low false positives. For example, when functional tests exercise a login flow, an IAST agent can show that a particular method failed to validate input coming from a parameter, and it can point to the exact file and line involved. That combination of code-level detail and runtime visibility reduces wasted developer time spent chasing false positives. However, IAST requires deployment of agents and relies on test coverage: if a function is never exercised, IAST cannot inspect it. Use IAST in QA or test environments where functional tests run frequently, and correlate IAST findings with SAST and DAST outputs to build confidence. One misconception is to treat IAST as a replacement for SAST or DAST — instead, treat it as a high-precision bridge that helps pinpoint remediations in complex applications. Interactive Application Security Testing (IAST) means iast combines runtime context with code visibility to produce accurate findings and direct remediation guidance.. In practical terms, instrumented runtime analysis that links code paths to live requests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Runtime Application Self-Protection is a defensive technology that runs inside the application and monitors behavior to detect and block attacks in real time. RASP acts like an immune system for the application: when it detects anomalies such as unexpected input patterns or sequences that match attack signatures, it can block requests, log evidence, and trigger alerts. A practical example is a RASP agent dropping a suspicious request that attempts a S Q L injection pattern and returning an error without exposing sensitive details. RASP is valuable in production because it provides immediate protection, including against zero-day techniques that reach the application. However, RASP can cause false positives if rules are too strict and may require tuning. It is not a substitute for fixing the underlying vulnerability; instead, treat RASP as mitigation and rapid response that reduces exposure while developers remediate the root cause. Consider RASP as a last-mile defense enabling safer production operations when combined with layered testing upstream. Penetration testing is a manual, goal-focused exercise performed by skilled security professionals to simulate real-world attacks. The objective is to find complex vulnerabilities, logical flaws, and chained exploit scenarios that automated tools often miss. For instance, testers may combine an authentication bypass, a misconfigured A P I and an exposed admin endpoint to demonstrate a full attack chain that has business impact. Penetration testing typically occurs later in the SDLC—before release or after major changes—to give a realistic assessment of the application's security posture. Key characteristics include manual creativity, targeted reconnaissance, and demonstrating exploitability and business impact. A common misconception is that automated scanners replace penetration testing; they do not. Automated tools surface many issues, but a human tester examines logic, workflows and context that tools cannot reason about. Use penetration tests to validate that automated controls work, to test business logic, and to provide prioritized findings with exploit scenarios. Fuzzing is a testing technique that bombards an application with malformed, unexpected or random inputs to reveal crashes, memory corruption, or other input-handling faults. It is particularly effective against parsers, protocol handlers, and file-processing code. A concrete example is feeding malformed files into a document parser to trigger a buffer overflow that an ordinary functional test would not reach. Fuzzing can be automated at scale and sometimes uncovers obscure vulnerabilities that remain hidden for years. One important point is that fuzzing often finds a symptom — a crash or exception — but not the root cause; developers must analyze the crash to fix the underlying bug. Also, fuzzing may produce many non-security-related crashes, so triage and reproducibility are critical. Use fuzzing in components that process untrusted input and combine it with sanitizers and memory analysis tools to get precise diagnostics. In short, fuzzing surfaces low-level failures that traditional AST techniques may miss. Integrating application security testing into CI/CD automates the tests developers need and transforms security from a bottleneck into a continuous assurance practice. A practical pipeline looks like this: run SAST on every commit or pull request to catch code-level issues early; after successful builds deploy to a staging environment and trigger a DAST scan to validate runtime behavior; during QA run IAST agents alongside functional tests to get high-precision findings; finally, schedule periodic penetration testing and fuzzing for deep, manual and low-level coverage. When interpreting results in an automated pipeline, prioritize failures that block builds differently from informational alerts: severe, exploitable issues may require blocking deployments, while low-confidence findings can be ticketed for scheduled fixes. Interpreting security test output is as critical as running the tests. A raw report can contain a mix of false positives, informational notes and high-confidence exploitable issues. Start triage by assessing three elements for each finding: severity, exploitability and business impact. Severity describes the technical consequence; exploitability answers whether an attacker can reach the vulnerability; business impact quantifies data loss, downtime or regulatory exposure. A concrete example is an exposed debug endpoint: it may have medium severity but high exploitability in production and a high business impact if it leaks credentials. Use those dimensions to decide if a finding should block a release, be scheduled for a patch, or accepted with compensating controls like RASP. Common mistakes include failing to retest after remediation or relying solely on a single tool's confidence score. These core concepts will help you architect practical security testing. First, Application Security Testing is an umbrella term for complementary methods that together provide coverage across code, runtime and production. Second, SAST analyzes code artifacts early to give precise remediation guidance, while DAST validates what attackers can reach at runtime; use them together rather than in isolation. Third, IAST and RASP add runtime context: IAST links execution to code for accurate findings during testing, and RASP provides active defense in production. Keep these three concepts in mind as you design pipelines and choose tools: layering methods reduces blind spots, automation makes testing scalable, and human-led tests provide depth where automation cannot reach. Ask yourself which gaps remain in your current process and which combination of methods will close them most effectively.

A few quick reminders as you apply these ideas. First, fuzzing complements AST by targeting low-level input handling and discovering crashes that other tests miss. Second, penetration testing provides human-led creativity to find chained exploits and to assess real-world impact. Third, effective prioritization requires triage based on severity, exploitability and business impact plus reproduction evidence and retest after fixes. Carry these reminders into your workflows: schedule fuzzing where parsers exist, budget pen tests for critical releases, and always attach repro steps to tickets to speed remediation. These practices turn test output into reduced risk and stronger applications.
